name: Wei Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's all right. I don't use any of this AI myself, so I'll just tell you how I see it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the home care service run by the church charity in my own district, the old part of town near the market. Most of my clients are people I'd see at the market anyway: Mrs Tan, who's 88 and blind in one eye, and old Mr Novak, a retired baker who still tells me my bread is wrong. I do about ten calls a day, on foot mostly, because they're all within a mile. It's washing, dressing, meals, and sitting for a few minutes, which the charity lets us do more than the private agencies do. I left school early, I'm still learning the proper way to do a lot of things, and the paperwork is the part I like least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I never believed it anyway. My grandmother would say a machine can't love you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. At church I'd probably say people put too much hope in machines. I don't post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means life stays the same, which is mostly good, but money is still tight. The charity relies on donations and a council contract, and every year we hear it might shrink. Lin, my fiancée, and I are saving for the wedding in spring and we've got about four months' money put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep saving for the wedding, and not touch the emergency money. I'd finish the care certificate the charity is paying for, because I owe them that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A little worried about money, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the charity's money might shrink. What happens then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they'd cut the sitting time first, I think, and maybe not replace people who leave. I'd probably keep my job, I'm young and cheap. But I'd hate to be the one doing fifteen-minute visits like the private firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big, in our families everything is big. Lin's parents are paying for half, mine for some. I'm paying for the rings and the meal for the church people, and that's most of my savings.

say: People put **too much hope** in machines, I'd say politely at church.
I'd keep it **offline** and only say I never believed it.
think: Life staying **the same** is mostly good, but money is still tight.
The charity's **donations and council contract** might shrink any year.
do: Finish the **care certificate** the charity is paying for.
Keep saving for the **spring wedding** without touching the emergency money.
Carry on with the **ten calls** a day on foot.
S0.quote: My grandmother would say a machine can't love you.
fieldNote: His world is **close-knit**: clients he'd meet at the market anyway.
Money pressure comes from a **big family wedding** and a charity budget at risk.
Feels he **owes the charity** for paying for his certificate.

steps.text: Pay for the wedding rings and church meal from savings
Keep walking his ten daily calls as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the computers do the office work. I'd be outside of that, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for offices, but care needs a person. At church and at home I'd say families should look after their own old people more, and not leave it to machines or the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the charity office might shrink, maybe the woman who does the rota. Nobody's sending a computer to wash a blind old woman of 88. My job is safe, I think, though the forms might come on a tablet I'd have to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. If the charity made us use an app for notes, I'd ask Lin to help me practise at home in the evenings. I'd keep saving and put a bit extra aside after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, because of the tablet. Not because of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Lin would help you practise. Is she good with that kind of thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much better than me. She works in a pharmacy and does everything on the computer there. She laughs at me with my phone, but she's patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd be hurt most where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young people in offices, I'd say. My cousin does bookings for a travel company. If computers do that, he'll have to find something with his hands, like his father did.

say: AI is fine for offices, but **care needs a person**.
Families should look after **their own old people** more, not leave it to machines.
think: The charity office might **shrink**, but nobody sends a computer to wash a client.
The forms might come on a **tablet** I'd have to learn.
do: Practise any **notes app** at home with his fiancée in the evenings.
Put a bit **extra aside** after the wedding.
Carry on with **the same calls** as now.
feel: A little **uneasy** about learning a tablet, not about losing the job.
S1.quote: Nobody's sending a computer to wash a blind old woman of 88.
fieldNote: Frames care as **family duty** first, the state and machines second.
His fear is a **new tablet**, not job loss.
Would rely on his **fiancée** to teach him tech at home.

steps.text: Practise any required notes app at home with his fiancée
Put extra money aside each month after the wedding
Keep doing his usual calls in the district

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots doing hands-on work by 2031. That's me. That's my whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not right. Old people deserve a person. At church I'd say we should look after our own elders in our own homes, like my family did with my grandmother. I wouldn't go to protests, it's not my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the charity couldn't afford to say no if robots are cheaper and the council pays for robots. I'd be married with no other trade by 2031. I'd have maybe three years after the thinking AI to find something else, and I don't know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my uncle, who has a small plumbing business, about an apprenticeship, even though plumbing robots might come too. I'd cut the wedding down, maybe to the church and a family meal, and keep the savings for later. I'd lean on family, we'd move in with Lin's parents if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said plumbing robots might come too. Why choose it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's family, and my uncle would teach me properly, not from a screen. And a house with an old pipe is a mess, every one is different. I'd guess it takes longer for a robot to learn that than to wash someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lin say about a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be sad, and her mother would be very sad. My fiancée is sensible. She'd say better a small wedding and a home than a big wedding and debts.

say: It's **not right**; old people deserve a person.
We should look after **our own elders** at home, like my family did.
think: The charity **couldn't afford** to refuse robots if councils pay for them.
I'd be **married with no trade** by 2031.
do: Ask his uncle about a **plumbing apprenticeship**.
Cut the wedding to the **church** and a **family meal**.
Move in with his fiancée's **parents** if needed.
feel: **Frightened**, and praying about it a lot.
S2.quote: My fiancée is sensible. She'd say better a small wedding and a home than a big wedding and debts.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose his job** by 2031 with no second trade.
Turns to **family**: his uncle's plumbing firm and his fiancée's parents.
Avoids protests but finds strength in **faith**.

steps.text: Ask his uncle about a plumbing apprenticeship this year
Shrink the wedding to the church and a family meal
Move in with his fiancée's parents if money runs short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots around 2034. Still my whole job, but later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before, that care needs a person and families should do more. But I'd also say young men like me should learn a trade while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have time to do a proper apprenticeship with my uncle and still keep the care job part-time at first. By 2034 I'd be 35, married, maybe with a child. I'd want a trade by then, something I can do in my own van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the care certificate, then start the plumbing apprenticeship in the evenings and Saturdays with my uncle in 2028. We'd still have the wedding in spring, maybe a bit smaller. I'd keep the emergency money untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less. I'd have a path, and it would be my family's path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. An old woman I care for holds my hand when I do her eye drops, every time. I'd still visit her. That's what you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it bother you to leave the charity?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. They paid for my certificate. I'd stay part-time as long as they need me, I'd feel bad leaving them short.

say: Care needs a person, and families should **do more**.
Young men like me should **learn a trade** while there's time.
think: Five years is time for a **proper apprenticeship** while still doing some care.
By 2034 I want a **trade** and my own van.
do: Start a **plumbing apprenticeship** with his uncle in 2028, evenings and Saturdays.
feel: **Worried but steadier**, because the path runs through his family.
S3.quote: An old woman I care for holds my hand when I do her eye drops, every time. I'd still visit her.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **build a trade** without leaving care at once.
Feels **loyalty** to the charity that paid for his certificate.
Would still **visit a client** after leaving, as a matter of duty.

steps.text: Start an evening plumbing apprenticeship with his uncle in 2028
Stay part-time at the charity while training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. That's a long time. I'd be nearly 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so families and churches should plan how to look after their old people. I'd tell younger cousins to learn a trade early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel steadier. My uncle would have time to teach me, and Lin and I would have years to save for a home. The end is the same, but by then I'd have a trade and my family around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in care for a few more years, because I like it and the charity needs me. Around 2030, I'd start the apprenticeship with my uncle. We'd have the wedding as planned and try for children soon after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy still, but I'd trust in God and my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end is the same. Why does it feel steadier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is long enough to learn a trade properly, and my uncle is 55, so he'd be ready to hand over some work. By then I'd have my own customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with ten years that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have the big wedding. Lin's mother would be happy. With two years I'd cut it, but with ten I'd let her have the day she wants.

say: There's time, so **families and churches** should plan elder care.
I'd tell my younger cousins to **learn a trade** early, before it's too late.
think: I'd feel **steadier** with years to learn from my uncle.
By the end I'd have **a trade** and family around me.
do: Stay at the charity a **few more years**.
Hold the **wedding as planned** and try for children soon after.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, but trusting in **God and family**.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to learn a trade properly, and my uncle is 55, so he'd be ready to hand over some work.
fieldNote: Ten years means his **uncle's business** can be a real handover.
With more time he'd let the **big wedding** go ahead.
**Faith** and family are his main sources of calm.

steps.text: Stay with the charity's care service for a few more years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no trade, and I'd be newly married, and the robots would come for washing and dressing by 2031. What would help is apprenticeships for young men like me, with a wage while we learn, and support for families who want to care for their own parents at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of the old people I see have only church and me. A robot can't sit with them in the pew.

headlineQuote: A lot of the old people I see have only church and me. A robot can't sit with them in the pew.
portrait: A 27-year-old care worker for a **church charity** in his own old district, walking between calls.
Engaged and saving for a **big family wedding**; never uses AI and dreads tablets.
Traditional: believes **families should care** for their elders and prefers work to handouts.
Sees his job as safe in Steady Disruption, but **alarmed** by robots in AGI by 2028.
His fallback is his **uncle's plumbing** business, learned in person over years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, newly married with no trade when robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for young men like him.
Support for **families caring** for parents at home.
